lines.text: Why is the east side of so many old English cities the poorer side?
From London to the mill towns of the north, it happens again and again. And the reason isn't on the ground. It's in the air.
Most days, Britain's wind blows in from the west, off the Atlantic Ocean, right across the country to the North Sea.
Then came the factories, burning coal. Researchers have mapped about 5,000 of their chimneys in England's cities in the eighteen eighties.
And the west wind did what wind does. It carried all that smoke east, over the streets downwind, day after day. So who had to breathe it?
Families who could pay moved upwind, into big houses with gardens on the clean west side.
Workers who couldn't stayed east, in cheap terraced streets under the soot, breathing everyone else's smoke.
Then the mills closed, and the air cleared. And the strange part? The split stayed.
Rich streets kept pulling in rich families, and cheap streets kept pulling in the poor, long after the smoke was gone, generation after generation.
In 2011, more than a century later, that old smoke still explains up to 20% of how England's neighbourhoods split into rich and poor.
